The King dory (Cyttus traversi) is a moderately deep-bodied zeiform fish inhabiting continental slope waters off southern Australia and New Zealand. Field surveys indicate that this species attains a maximum recorded total length of 63 centimeters [Li = 63 centimeters], a figure derived from extensive trawl sampling across its geographic range. Adult body mass corresponding to this ultimate length has been estimated from length-weight regressions, yielding an asymptotic wet weight of 5000 grams [Wwi = 5000 grams], placing Cyttus traversi among the larger members of the family Zeidae. Growth increment data from otolith readings suggest that individuals approach this asymptotic size relatively slowly, which is consistent with the prolonged maximum lifespan observed in this species. Under typical thermal conditions at depth, where water temperatures hover near 8.3 °C [T = 8.3 °C], the maximum recorded longevity has been estimated at approximately 38 years [am = approximately 38 years], a figure derived from validated annulus counts in sagittal otoliths from older individuals captured off the Chatham Rise. Such longevity is remarkable for a demersal teleost of this body size and likely reflects the low metabolic demands imposed by the cold, stable environment of the upper continental slope.

Reproductive biology in Cyttus traversi follows a pattern of delayed maturation and moderate fecundity characteristic of slow-growing, deep-water zeiforms. Puberty is attained at a total length of 21.6 centimeters [Lp = 21.6 centimeters], a threshold corresponding to a wet weight at puberty of 196.5 grams [Wwp = 196.5 grams] based on the length-weight conversion established for this species. Histological examination of gonad tissue from individuals collected during the spawning season revealed a gonadosomatic index (GSI) of 3.48% [GSI = 3.48%] when measured at a water temperature of 8.3 °C [T = 8.3 °C]. This reproductive strategy may be an adaptive response to the relatively low and predictable food availability typical of its bathybenthic habitat.

Early life history in King dory commences with the fertilisation of pelagic eggs, which are approximately 0.8 millimeters in diameter. The developing yolk-laden embryo undergoes a period of incubation within the chorion before eclosion, with hatching occurring after 17 days [ab = 17 days] at a temperature of 8.3 °C [T = 8.3 °C]. Upon emergence, the yolk-sac larva is extremely small, with a computed wet weight at birth of approximately 0.000268 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.000268 grams], a minute body size that reflects the modest provisioning of yolk reserves relative to the small egg diameter. This lecithotrophic stage persists until the onset of exogenous feeding, at which point the mouth-closed larva undergoes the trophic switch and begins active prey capture. The protracted incubation period relative to egg size may be a consequence of the low ambient temperatures characteristic of the species' spawning grounds, where developmental rates are substantially slowed. Following yolk-sac resorption, the prolarva transitions into a planktonic juvenile phase.

Comparative studies within the Zeidae shed light on the life-history strategy of Cyttus traversi relative to its better-studied congener Zeus faber. While both species share similar maximum body dimensions, the King dory exhibits a notably extended juvenile phase before reaching the total length at puberty of 21.6 centimeters [Lp = 21.6 centimeters]. The developmental trajectory from hatching to this pubertal milestone appears to be governed by the cold thermal regime, as both the incubation period of 17 days [ab = 17 days] and the maximum lifespan of approximately 38 years [am = approximately 38 years] were recorded under equivalent temperature conditions of 8.3 °C [T = 8.3 °C]. This thermal control over developmental rate is consistent with the broader pattern observed in deep-water marine teleosts, where reduced metabolic rates at low temperatures lead to extended pre-reproductive periods and increased longevity. The 5000-gram ultimate wet weight (5000 grams) [Wwi = 5000 grams] represents a substantial body mass that is achieved only after many years of continuous growth, suggesting that iteroparous spawning over several decades is the typical life-history pathway for this species.

Ecologically, Cyttus traversi occupies a demersal niche on the continental slope at depths between 200 and 800 meters, where it preys primarily on mesopelagic fishes and squids. The slow life-history pace characterized by a 38-year lifespan (38 years) [am = 38 years] and late pubertal maturation at 196.5 grams [Wwp = 196.5 grams] wet weight is matched by a low natural mortality rate, consistent with the predictions of the metabolic theory of ecology for cold-water ectotherms at a temperature of 8.3 °C [T = 8.3 °C]. The gonadosomatic index was 3.48% [GSI = 3.48%], and each hatchling weighs 0.000268 grams [Wwb = 0.000268 grams] at a temperature of 8.3 °C [T = 8.3 °C]. The ultimate total length of 63 centimeters [Li = 63 centimeters] serves as the upper bound of an asymptotic growth trajectory that is rarely attained given the pressures of commercial bycatch mortality, but in unexploited populations this species exemplifies a K-selected life history adapted to stable, low-productivity environments.
